newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN SOCIALISTS MEET, PROTESTERS BLOCK ROADS.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN SOCIALISTS MEET, PROTESTERS BLOCK ROADS.

text.p: Protesters blocked main roads around Bulgaria on Sunday as leaders of the ruling Socialist Party met to try to form a new government, ignoring four weeks of daily opposition rallies and calls for immediate elections.

Bulgaria is edging towards economic collapse and urgently needs a credible government to negotiate with foreign lenders and set up a tough fixed exchange rate regime to restore confidence in the national currency.

Delegates at the meeting said critics of outgoing premier Zhan Videnov, who resigned in December, were pressing for the deeply divided party to return its mandate, paving the way for a general election, but hardliners were resisting the call.
"We are not going to give up power," said executive bureau member Valentin Vatsev.
The main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) resolutely opposes any new Socialist-led cabinet and wants an immediate general election.
Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, the Socialists' nominee for premier, tried on Friday to propose a compromise way out but failed to win the backing of the party leadership.
At Doupnitsa, 60 km (35 miles) south of Sofia, several hundred opposition supporters blocked road and rail links to Greece for a fifth day.
Protesters warmed themselves at wood fires on barricades and said that if the Socialists formed a new cabinet they would set up their barricades outside parliament.
Miners and steelworkers went on strike, and protesters blocked main roads around the second city of Plovdiv and the highway to the border with the former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia.
State radio said distribution staff at the Neftohim refinery were operating only a minimum service, supplying schools, hospitals and the police.
Thousands of opposition supporters, workers and students, blaming the Socialists for the economic collapse, have staged daily anti-government rallies since January 6 to demand elections.
They accuse the Socialists and their powerful business allies of carrying out only superficial reforms, while siphoning public money abroad.

Socialist Party leader Georgi Parvanov said in a television interview on Saturday: "I'm sure next week Bulgaria will have a new government but it is hard to predict what the future of this government will be."
The Socialists say they will hold general elections, not due until December 1998, later this year. Their offer failed to satisfy the opposition, which wants the vote held now.

The party has until Tuesday to come up with a cabinet. If they present a list to parliament for approval, many people fear a repeat of the violence which broke out between police and demonstrators after opposition protesters besieged and ransacked parliament on January 10.
President Petar Stoyanov, who has tried to mediate a compromise, has called on the Socialists to give up their mandate and agree to immediate elections.
Dobrev suggested on Friday that Stoyanov appoint a coalition cabinet but then put off a meeting with him, apparently under pressure from party hardliners.
